title: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
hook: a tightrope walker's pole never stops moving; one line in the Ashtanga Hridaya puts health on the same wire
carry: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis, took two questions: prakriti, the banks of the river, and vikriti, the water level after the storm. Did you ask the second one, how am I today? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

A tightrope walker is never quite still. Watch the long pole in their hands: it dips a little left, a little right, catching each tilt before it turns into a fall. From the ground it looks like calm. Up on the wire it's a steady run of small corrections. Balance, up there, isn't a pose someone strikes once and keeps. It's something done again and again. The Ashtanga Hridaya puts health on that same wire, in a single short line. On the last of the dosha days: balance, not a type.
screen: `A POLE THAT NEVER STOPS MOVING.` → `SMALL CORRECTIONS.` → `ONE LINE ON BALANCE.`

segments.voice: Here is the line, in paraphrase: illness is the doshas out of balance; health is the doshas in balance. Two halves, one the mirror of the other. In Sanskrit the key words are vaishamya, unevenness, and samya, evenness. Now look at what the line leaves out. It doesn't ask for less of any dosha. Vata, the moving one, still moves the breath. Pitta, the hot one, still digests the meal. Kapha, the steady one, still holds the body together. Health isn't one of them winning, or one of them being driven out. It's the three of them even with each other. And the line doesn't sort anyone. It doesn't say health is being a vata person or a kapha person. It describes the three together, in balance or out of it, in any body. That gathers up the dosha days. The three as forces. Their qualities, dry and heavy and hot. Their turns on the clock. Like adding to like. A nature that holds and a today that changes. Every one of those was a way of seeing which way things are tipping. Here is where the title earns its second half. In the classical texts, judging an imbalance is a physician's work, done by examining a person closely. A lesson can't do that, and neither can a quiz. Pain, fever, a change that worries you: that goes to a doctor. What the line offers an ordinary day is smaller, and it travels. Not what's wrong with me. Just: what's tipping right now, and what small correction would bring it a little nearer the middle?
screen: `ILLNESS: THE DOSHAS UNEVEN` · `HEALTH: THE DOSHAS EVEN` · `ALL THREE STAY` · `NOTICING, NOT DIAGNOSING`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the middle, and keep finding it. Sit upright, feet on the floor. Let the body lean a little to the left, then a little to the right, like the walker's pole. Make each sway smaller than the last, until you settle somewhere near the center. Stay there and feel the tiny adjustments that keep you upright, the ones you usually never notice. Then let the breath find its own middle: the in-breath and the out-breath, about the same length, without forcing. If you pray, you can rest in prayer here. The bell holds the time.

The three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. In the Ashtanga Hridaya's line, illness is the three out of balance, and health is the three in balance: an evenness kept by small corrections. Today's word.

Your line: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Today, when something tips, a rushed hour, a hot reply, a heavy afternoon, make one small correction toward the middle. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Ayurvedic practitioners describe health as the three doshas in balance and illness as their imbalance, and some people who follow Ayurveda use the idea to notice daily patterns alongside medical care, not in place of it.

fork.setup: vata feels loud today: rushing, scattered, dry. on the line from the Ashtanga Hridaya, what are you aiming for?
options: the three a little more even with each other.
fork.reveal: the line puts health in the doshas' balance, not in removing one. a small correction toward the middle is the whole move.

original.note: Sanskrit samya: evenness, sameness. In the Ashtanga Hridaya, the doshas in samya, in balance, is health.

trapdoor: what you thought: health means finding your type, or getting rid of a bad dosha.
what it means: health is the three in balance, an evenness kept by small corrections, with all three still at work.
what a scholar hears: rogas tu dosha-vaishamyam, dosha-samyam arogata, 'illness is the doshas uneven; health is the doshas even.'
